blocks.content: A process is a program in execution. The moment you double click an application or run a command, the operating system creates a process for it, giving it its own memory, its own resources, and a place in line for the processor.

This topic explains precisely what a process is, how it differs from the program stored on disk, what state it carries, and why the operating system treats every running program as a first class object it must track.

A program is a passive set of instructions stored on disk, like an executable file. It does nothing on its own. A process is that program loaded into memory and actively running, with its own allocated resources: memory, open files, and a current execution position.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A program is a file on disk, a process is that program actually running, with memory and resources allocated to it.
Every process the operating system creates carries a specific bundle of information with it, tracked for as long as the process exists.

["Memory space: code, data, and a stack and heap for the running program.","Process state: whether it is ready, running, or waiting.","Program counter: which instruction the process will execute next.","CPU registers: the current values the processor is working with for this process.","Open resources: files, network connections, and other handles the process is using."]
items: Memory space: code, data, and a stack and heap for the running program.
Process state: whether it is ready, running, or waiting.
Program counter: which instruction the process will execute next.
CPU registers: the current values the processor is working with for this process.
Open resources: files, network connections, and other handles the process is using.

blocks.content: 3. Why the Operating System Tracks Processes
blocks.text: 3. Why the Operating System Tracks Processes

blocks.content: Multiple processes typically want the processor at the same time, and the operating system must be able to pause one and resume another without losing any of its progress. This is only possible because every process's full state is tracked separately.
A process is the operating system's unit of execution and the unit of resource ownership, everything a running program needs is bundled into its process.

A common interview question asks you to define a process and immediately follow up asking how it differs from a thread. Being able to state precisely what state a process owns, memory, open files, and execution context, is what signals real understanding rather than a memorized definition.
